name: Nora Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Nora. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group with no ties to tech companies, employers, unions or government. Nothing you say will carry your name, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: This time of year it's pruning. Our family has the orchard at Hillcrest, twenty-eight hectares of apples and pears, my grandfather planted the oldest trees. I'm out by half seven with my dad and two of our regulars, Ernesto and old Bill, each of us with a ladder and loppers, working down a row. You learn every tree. I love it, the quiet, the cold air. What wears me out is the cold store paperwork and the packhouse rejecting fruit for little marks that don't change the taste one bit.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use AI tools for any of that?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No. Never have. Dad's got the weather app on his phone, that's as far as we go. I live in the little house at the bottom of the orchard. I'm courting Josh, he's a joiner, we met at chapel. We've got about three months' money saved between the orchard's slow months, that's mine, not the farm's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Well, that sounds about right to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. People get excited about every new gadget. A tree takes seven years to bear properly, and no computer is changing that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be glad. I don't want my life to change. I want to prune the trees my grandfather planted and pass them on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. Prune in winter, blossom in spring, pick in September. Maybe Dad would let the packhouse do the paperwork on their computer system and save me an evening. We'd keep putting a bit by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's your worry in this picture, if it isn't AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Prices. The supermarkets and the cheap imports. We get less for a box of apples than we did when I was ten. That's what's hurting us, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you hold responsible for that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not the shoppers. People are pinched. I'd say the big buyers, and the government for piling forms and rules on small growers. Let us get on with it.

S0.say: I'd say I'm not surprised, because people get excited about every gadget. A tree takes seven years to bear properly and no computer changes that.
S0.think: Privately she'd be glad, because she doesn't want her life to change. She wants to prune her grandfather's trees and pass them on.
S0.do: Carries on with the orchard year as usual, from winter pruning to September picking. Lets the packhouse handle paperwork on its system and keeps saving a little.
S0.quote: A tree takes seven years to bear properly, and no computer is changing that.
S0.fieldNote: Nora sees the orchard as a family line, not just a job. She blames big buyers and government rules for her troubles, never shoppers. She's content in a world that stays the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hm. I don't much like the sound of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farming is about families and know-how, not gadgets, and the government shouldn't be pushing robots on growers with grants. Let people choose. That's what I'd say at the growers' group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I know picking robots for apples are already being tried. If the big orchards get them, they'll sell cheaper, and we can't keep up. That's what really frightens me. Not the robot. The price.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as we are, and wait to see if these machines actually work in a real orchard on a slope. I'd cut back on anything extra, keep the money in the bank. I might talk Dad into opening a pick-your-own on Saturdays, so people come for the day out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like seeing frost forecast in May.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Pick-your-own is an interesting idea. Where did that come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Josh's sister took her kids to one last autumn and paid more for a bag of apples than we get for a box. People will pay for the day, for the trees. A robot can't sell them that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ernesto and Bill, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them we're a family orchard and we look after our own. While I've any say, nobody gets a robot instead of them. Dad would say the same. I'd mean it.

S1.say: I'd say farming is about families and know-how, not gadgets, and the government shouldn't push robots on growers with grants. Let people choose.
S1.think: Privately she knows apple-picking robots are being tried, and big orchards using them could undercut her family's prices. The price scares her more than the machine.
S1.do: Keeps working as before and waits to see whether picking robots work on real sloped orchards. Cuts extra spending, holds savings and suggests a Saturday pick-your-own to her father.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like frost forecast in May.
S1.quote: That's what really frightens me. Not the robot. The price.
S1.fieldNote: She would resist change publicly, but her private fear is market prices, not technology itself. Her loyalty to the farm's two regular workers is strong and personal. Pick-your-own lets her earn from tradition rather than fight it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028? Lord. That's two pickings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's wrong. Not everything that can be done should be done. I'd say it at chapel, at the growers' group, to anyone. People are made to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think we'd lose the orchard. Not straight away. But if a robot orchard down the road sells for half, the packhouse stops taking ours, and Dad can't carry the debt. Three generations, and it'd go on my watch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd stop spending on anything but food and the farm. I'd talk to Josh about bringing the wedding forward and living small. I'd lean on chapel and family, that's what they're there for. We'd sell what we could direct, at the gate, at markets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. A sort of grief before anything's even happened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why bring the wedding forward?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because whatever happens, I want that settled. Josh is good with his hands, joinery's needed. If the orchard went, we'd have one wage and each other. That's a start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does only two years change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's no time to adjust, and I'm not quick at changing anyway. Two years, you can't even replant. All you can do is hold on and pray.

S2.say: I'd say it's wrong, because not everything that can be done should be done. She'd say at chapel and the growers' group that people are made to work.
S2.think: Privately she thinks the family would lose the orchard once a cheaper robot orchard undercut them and the packhouse stopped buying. Three generations would end on her watch.
S2.do: Cuts spending to food and farm costs only and brings forward her wedding to live small. Leans on chapel and family and sells fruit direct at the gate and at markets.
S2.feel: Alarmed, with a kind of grief before anything has happened.
S2.quote: Three generations, and it'd go on my watch.
S2.fieldNote: Her objection is moral as well as economic: people are made to work. Faced with fast change she turns to family, faith and marriage, not to the state. The guilt of being the generation that loses the land runs through every answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Still too quick, but better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same thing, that it's wrong to rush it. But I'd also say families and communities should get ready together, not wait for the government to fix it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years is enough to change what the orchard is for. Less packhouse, more people coming to us. Pick-your-own, our own juice and cider, the blossom in spring. Machines can make cheap apples. They can't make Hillcrest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd start pressing our own apple juice, Dad's been talking about it for years. We'd sell it at the farmers' market and the chapel fair. I'd put savings toward a small press, a few thousand. And I'd keep Ernesto and Bill on as long as there was work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with something to get on with. That helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd buy a juice press, but you'd never use AI tools. Is that a contradiction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. A press is a machine I understand, like a ladder. AI I don't understand and I don't want it making my choices. Josh would probably set something up for the orders, and that's his business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about most in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bill. He's sixty-one and he's never done anything else. He's like an uncle. I'd want to keep him as long as I possibly could, even if it cost us.

S3.say: I'd say it's wrong to rush it, and that families and communities should get ready together rather than wait for the government. That's what she'd say in public.
S3.think: Privately she thinks five years is enough to turn the orchard toward visitors, juice, cider and blossom days. Machines can make cheap apples, but not Hillcrest.
S3.do: Starts pressing and selling the family's own apple juice at markets and fairs, spending a few thousand of her savings on a small press. Keeps the two regular workers on as long as there's work.
S3.feel: Anxious, but steadier for having something to get on with.
S3.quote: Machines can make cheap apples. They can't make Hillcrest.
S3.fieldNote: With five years she shifts from holding on to building something from what the family already has. She's comfortable with machines she understands and wary of ones that decide. Loyalty to an older worker shapes her spending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Dad would be near seventy. I'd have the orchard by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is time to do it right, through families and apprenticeships, not handouts. Teach the young ones the trade and the business both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd probably drag my feet. Ten years feels like forever when you're pruning one tree at a time. I'd believe it about year six, and then I'd be in a hurry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the orchard going as it is, build up the juice and pick-your-own slowly. Josh and I would marry and, God willing, start a family. I'd save a bit more each year. Maybe plant some new rows of old varieties people can't get in shops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Uneasy underneath, because I know I'd leave it late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why old varieties?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because they're what a person can sell that a big robot orchard won't bother with. Twenty kinds, all different. Nobody's going to programme a robot for that. Or maybe they will. But I'd bet on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does ten years compare with two for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, I'd lose it all and grieve. Ten years, I'd have a family and a plan by the end. But I'd waste the first five, I know I would. Somebody would need to shake me.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is time to do it right through families and apprenticeships, not handouts. Young people should learn the trade and the business both.
S4.think: Privately she'd drag her feet, because ten years feels like forever when pruning one tree at a time. She'd only believe it around year six and then rush.
S4.do: Keeps the orchard running as it is while slowly building juice and pick-your-own sales. Marries her partner, plans a family, saves more each year and plants rows of old apple varieties.
S4.feel: Mostly calm but uneasy underneath, knowing she'd leave it late.
S4.quote: Ten years feels like forever when you're pruning one tree at a time.
S4.fieldNote: Like other resistant workers, she sees a long warning as a temptation to wait. Her plans centre on family and heritage: marriage, children, old varieties. She expects to need a push from someone close.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. We'd lose the orchard in two pickings, and I'd be the one who lost it. What would help is fewer rules on small growers selling direct, so we can sell juice and fruit at the gate without a pile of forms, and apprenticeships so young people learn the trade from people like Dad.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. For some of us, work isn't just money, it's what we're for. If machines do all the work, what are people for? I'd want somebody to ask that question seriously.

headlineQuote: Machines can make cheap apples. They can't make Hillcrest.
portrait: Nora Reyes is a 27-year-old who works her family's 28-hectare apple and pear orchard alongside her father and two long-standing workers, and has never used an AI tool. She's engaged in all but name to Josh, a joiner she met at chapel, and has about three months saved. She's traditional and free-market, blaming big buyers and government rules rather than shoppers, and sees work as part of what people are for. In the fast AGI picture she expects to lose the orchard and leans on faith, family and marriage. With more warning she turns the orchard toward juice, pick-your-own and old varieties, though she admits she'd leave it late.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because the family orchard could be lost within two pickings and she would be the generation that lost it.
whatWouldHelp: Fewer rules on small growers selling direct, and apprenticeships so young people learn the trade from experienced growers.
